claim: CT has two income tax liens. On real estate, the lien arises automatically from the last day of the taxable year and lasts until payment. DRS may record a certificate of it with the town clerk. On personal property (goods, accounts, deposit accounts, intangibles), the state gets a lien when tax is unpaid 30 days after its due date. That lien attaches only when a notice is filed under UCC Article 9. Neither statute sets a minimum amount.

realEstate.arises: automatically, from the last day of the taxable year until discharged by payment
realEstate.perfectedBy: certificate of lien filed for record with the clerk of the town where the real estate lies

personalProperty.arises: failure to pay within 30 days of the due date, or earlier on jeopardy
personalProperty.perfectedBy: notice filed under UCC Article 9 part 5 (Secretary of the State)

sourceDate: CGS revised to January 1, 2025 (page notes a 2026 Supplement); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: CGS 12-734: 'The amount of any such tax, penalty and interest shall be a lien, from the last day of the taxable year until discharged by payment, against all real estate of the taxpayer within the state, and a certificate of such lien signed by the commissioner may be filed for record in the office of the clerk of any town in which such real estate is situated.' CGS 12-35a(b) (https://www.cga.ct.gov/current/pub/chap_202.htm): 'Upon failure of any person to pay any tax ... due the state within thirty days from its due date ... the state shall have a lien, upon perfection ... upon the goods, accounts, ... deposit accounts ... and general intangibles.'
uncertainty: The real-estate lien is invalid against a bona fide purchaser or qualified encumbrancer until it is recorded. No minimum amount is stated anywhere. Whether DRS files only above some internal amount is NOT FOUND.
designImplication: For CT, an unpaid income tax balance is a lien on real estate from the start. The game event is the recording, not the lien arising. Gate a personal-property lien on 30 days unpaid past the due date.

claim: No statute or DRS publication found names a notice that must come before a lien is recorded. The Taxpayer Bill of Rights promises at least 30 days' notice before collection actions 'which require sale or seizure of property or freezing of assets'. The 30-day written notice of intent in CGS 12-35(b) is for a warrant on intangible property, such as a bank or wage levy, not for a lien. DRS says 'generally' it gives at least 30 days' notice of its intent to take civil enforcement action.
establishes: PS 2008(4) p.3: 'Generally, DRS will give you at least 30 days notice of our intent to take civil enforcement action. If you fully pay your tax obligation within the 30-day period, no enforcement action will be taken.' CGS 12-39n(5): 'the right to at least thirty days' notice in which to pay the liability or seek further review' for collection actions that require sale or seizure of property or freezing of assets.
uncertainty: Whether the 30-day notice of intent covers recording a lien, which is not a seizure, is not stated. PS 2008(4) is dated 2009. No later Taxpayer Bill of Rights policy statement was found.
designImplication: Model CT as a 30-day warning before 'civil enforcement'. Do not claim a lien-specific notice for CT.

claim: A real-estate lien certificate is recorded with the clerk of the town where the property lies (CGS 12-734). A personal-property lien notice is filed with the Secretary of the State under UCC Article 9. A discharge of it is filed with the UCC Division of the Secretary of the State (CGS 12-35a(b), (g)). No source found says what recording fee, if any, is charged to the taxpayer.

value.personalPropertyOffice: Secretary of the State, UCC Division

establishes: CGS 12-35a(g): the discharge certificate 'shall be filed with the Uniform Commercial Code Division of the office of the Secretary of the State in the same manner as termination statements are filed under section 42a-9-513.' CGS 12-35b(b): 'No town clerk shall refuse to record any such certificate because the commissioner has used an electronic signature thereon.'
uncertainty: CGS 12-35(a)(3)(B) adds serving-officer fees to a warrant. That is a levy cost, not a lien recording fee. No town-clerk fee passed to the taxpayer was found.
designImplication: Record CT liens at the town level for real estate and with the state for personal property. Charge no CT lien recording fee until one is sourced.

claim: The real-estate lien attaches to all of the taxpayer's real estate in CT and runs until discharged by payment. The personal-property lien attaches to goods, accounts, chattel paper, instruments, documents, investment property, deposit accounts, commercial tort claims and general intangibles. That includes after-acquired property. It is 'effective for a period of ten years from the date of filing unless discharged'. Separately, DRS may not collect a tax more than ten years after it was reported on a return or after an assessment became final. The unpaid tax is then abated.

realEstate.attachesTo: all real estate of the taxpayer within the state

establishes: CGS 12-35a(d): 'The lien shall be effective for a period of ten years from the date of filing unless discharged as hereinafter provided.' CGS 12-35(c)(1)(B) and (c)(2): tax not collected within ten years after an assessment became final 'shall be deemed abated as of the first day of the eleventh year'.
uncertainty: CGS 12-734 states no expiry for the real-estate lien itself. The ten-year collection limit in 12-35(c) caps it in practice, but no source found says the lien is released when the tax is abated.
designImplication: Give a CT personal-property lien a ten-year clock from filing. Cap a CT real-estate lien at the ten-year collection limit.

claim: After a lien's tax is satisfied, DRS issues a certificate discharging it 'upon request of any interested party' (CGS 12-734; 12-35a(g)). DRS's own policy statement says the taxpayer is responsible for recording the Certificate of Release. No deadline in days after payment was found, and no release fee was found. If DRS finds a lien was placed in error, it releases the lien and issues a statement saying so.

value.erroneousFiling: DRS releases it and issues a statement that it was placed in error

establishes: PS 2008(4) right 9: 'Upon full payment of your tax obligations, we will issue a Certificate of Release, but you are responsible for having the Certificate of Release recorded.' CGS 12-734: 'the commissioner, upon request of any interested party, shall issue a certificate discharging such lien, which certificate shall be recorded in the same office in which the lien was recorded.' The error statement is from superseded PS 92(4.1) (https://portal.ct.gov/DRS/Publications/Policy-Statements/1992/PS-92-4-1): 'If we find the lien was placed in error, we will release the lien and issue a statement indicating it was placed in error.'
uncertainty: The statute says only that the discharge 'shall be recorded'. That the taxpayer does the recording comes from the policy statement. The error-statement wording is from a superseded 1995 statement. The current one keeps the right but not that sentence.
designImplication: A CT release costs the player an action: request the certificate, then record it. Do not auto-release on payment.

claim: The CT Taxpayer Bill of Rights gives a right to procedures for requesting cancellation, release or modification of a DRS lien. It also gives a right to have a lien filed in error noted as such on the cancellation, in public notice and, at the taxpayer's request, in notice to any credit agency. The procedure's steps and a number of days were not found.

value.processNote: NOT FOUND (statute grants a right to 'procedures'; none published was found)

establishes: CGS 12-39n(9): 'The right to procedures for requesting cancellation, release or modification of liens filed by the department and for requesting that any lien which is filed in error be so noted on the lien cancellation filed by the department, in public notice and in notice to any credit agency at the taxpayer's request.'
uncertainty: 12-39n states that it grants no rights beyond other statutes. No DRS form or deadline for a lien challenge was found.
designImplication: Let a CT player contest a lien with no deadline. On success, the cancellation says 'filed in error'.

claim: DRS says a lien may be placed even while a payment plan is approved. No source says a plan requires a lien, and none says a lien is withheld or released while a plan is current.

value.lienRequiredNote: NOT FOUND (DRS 'may' file; no rule requiring it)

establishes: PS 2008(4) p.4: 'A tax lien may be placed on your property to secure our ability to collect the tax even if a payment plan is approved.' Also: 'If your payment plan is modified, we will give you 30 days notice before any changes become effective.'
uncertainty: The DRS Installment Agreement page (portal.ct.gov/DRS/Individuals/Individual-Tax-Page/Installment-Agreement) returned 404 on 2026-10-11. A search snippet of it gave a 12-month, $50,000 cap that could not be confirmed.
designImplication: In CT, a payment plan does not protect against a lien. Model lien filing as independent of plan status.

claim: A real-estate lien certificate is recorded in the town land records, which are public. A personal-property lien is filed as a UCC record with the Secretary of the State. No DRS source names any effect of the lien being public beyond its priority over later liens.

value.stateNamedEffect: priority over all subsequently perfected liens and security interests (personal property)

establishes: CGS 12-35a(b): 'upon perfection, such lien shall have priority over all subsequently perfected liens and security interests.'
uncertainty: That land records and UCC filings are public is general law, not a DRS statement found in this pass.
designImplication: For CT, the effect of recording is priority over later creditors. Do not invent other public effects.

claim: In NY the lien is the tax warrant. The Department may issue a warrant if assessed income tax is unpaid 21 calendar days after notice and demand. If the amount demanded is $100,000 or more, the period is 10 business days. It must issue the warrant within six years of the assessment. From July 1, 2025, the electronic filing of the warrant with the Department of State creates the lien. Nothing is automatic on assessment.

value.lienCreatedBy: electronic filing with the Department of State (Tax Law 6), from 2025-07-01

sourceDate: Tax Law 692 as displayed by the NY Senate; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Tax Law 692(c): if a person 'neglects or refuses to pay the same within twenty-one calendar days after notice and demand ... (ten business days if the amount for which such notice and demand is made equals or exceeds one hundred thousand dollars), the commissioner may within six years after the date of such assessment issue a warrant.' Tax Law 6 (https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/TAX/6): on electronic filing, 'the amount of the tax stated in the warrant shall become a lien upon the title to and interest in all real, personal or other property located in New York state.'
uncertainty: The DTF page (tax-warrants.htm, updated July 8, 2025) says only that a warrant is filed when the debt 'becomes fixed and final' and is not timely resolved. It gives no minimum amount.
designImplication: For NY, a warrant becomes possible 21 days after the notice and demand. Use 10 business days when the balance is $100,000 or more. The warrant itself is the lien.

claim: The notice before a NY warrant is the statutory 'notice and demand' for assessed tax (Tax Law 692(b)). The warrant clock runs from it: 21 calendar days, or 10 business days at $100,000 or more. DTF's online-services page lists a 'Notice and Demand series'. DTF says that before filing a warrant 'we will send you notice of the debt and give you an opportunity to resolve it.' No separate notice of intent to file a warrant was found.

value.noticeName: Notice and Demand (for Payment of Tax Due)
value.formNote: NOT FOUND on an official page (a search snippet gave DTF-966-E; unconfirmed)

establishes: tax-warrants.htm: 'Before we file a tax warrant, we will send you notice of the debt and give you an opportunity to resolve it.' Tax Law 692(b): 'The tax commission shall as soon as practicable give notice to each person liable for any amount of tax ... which has been assessed but remains unpaid.' https://www.tax.ny.gov/online/electronic-notices.htm lists a 'Notice and Demand series'.
uncertainty: The form number of the notice and demand is unconfirmed.
designImplication: NY needs one notice with a 21-day fuse, then the warrant. There is no second warning.

claim: From July 1, 2025, DTF files every warrant and warrant-related record electronically with the NY Department of State. That covers satisfactions, vacaturs, amendments and expirations. That filing creates a statewide lien. A copy also goes to the clerk of the county named in the warrant. Since July 1, 2025 the county copy is for information only. The law says 'No fee shall be required to be paid for such filings.' Before that date, a warrant was docketed by the county clerk, and it reached personal property only if it was also filed with the Department of State.

value.alsoFiledWith: county clerk named in the warrant (informational from 2025-07-01)
value.feeBasis: Tax Law 6: no fee for such filings
value.pre2025: county clerk judgment docket; personal property only if also filed with the Department of State (Tax Law 692(d))

sourceDate: Tax Law 6 as displayed by the NY Senate; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Tax Law 6: 'All warrants and warrant-related records issued by the department shall be filed electronically by the department in the department of state.' 'No fee shall be required to be paid for such filings.' Copies are 'filed by the department in the office of the clerk of the county named in the warrant or warrant-related record.' Department of State (https://dos.ny.gov/state-tax-warrant-notice-system): 'On or after July 1, 2025, all warrants are filed with the Department of State and the search displays the information constituting the official warrant.'
uncertainty: That county filings after July 1, 2025 are 'for informational purposes only' comes from county-clerk and title-company notices, which are secondary (e.g. https://www.nycourts.gov/LegacyPDFS/COURTS/12jd/bronx/countyclerk/nys-tax-law.pdf). Tax Law 6 itself says the Department of State filing creates the lien. Tax Law 692(f) limits officer fees to actual expenses of executing a warrant. That is not a filing fee.
designImplication: For NY, record the warrant at one statewide registry with no fee to the taxpayer. The county copy carries no legal weight.

claim: A filed NY warrant is a lien on the title to and interest in all real, personal or other property in New York owned by the person named, and it is deemed a judgment. A tax liability is extinguished 20 years from the first date a warrant could have been filed, whether or not one was. If no warrant is filed within six years of assessment, the 20-year rule does not apply and the liability is extinguished. DTF says that under an installment agreement the warrant stays a lien until the warranted balance is paid.

value.attachesTo: all real, personal or other property located in NY
value.from: first date a warrant could be filed

sourceDate: Tax Law 174-b as displayed by FindLaw; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Tax Law 174-b(1): 'every tax liability shall be extinguished after twenty years from the first date a warrant could be filed by the commissioner, without regard to whether the warrant is filed.' 174-b(4): 'if the commissioner does not file a warrant within six years of assessment ... the tax liability is extinguished.' Tax Law 6: the commissioner 'shall ... be deemed to have obtained a judgment against the person or persons named in the warrant.'
uncertainty: 174-b was read on FindLaw, a secondary host, not the official NY Senate site. The 'expirations' that Tax Law 6 says are filed were not tied to a specific number of years in any source read.
designImplication: For NY, a warrant runs about 20 years from 21 days after the notice and demand. That is far longer than other states, and it should feel that way.

claim: Once the full warranted balance is paid, DTF sends the Department of State and the county clerk a Satisfaction of Judgment. The taxpayer does not have to ask. No deadline in days after payment was found, and no release fee was found (Tax Law 6 says no fee is required for warrant-related filings, satisfactions included). Tax Law 6 also requires vacaturs to be filed. A process or deadline for vacating an erroneous warrant was not found.

value.releaseFeeBasis: Tax Law 6: no fee for warrant-related filings
value.erroneousFiling: vacatur filed with the Department of State (Tax Law 6); process and days NOT FOUND
value.partialReleaseOfProperty: Tax Law 692(i): may release property if the state's interest is not jeopardized

establishes: tax-warrants.htm: 'Once you pay your total warranted balance, we will send the New York State Department of State and the applicable county clerk a Satisfaction of Judgment stating you have paid your warranted debt in full.' Also: 'We can provide a copy of your Satisfaction of Judgment only after the New York State Department of State has received and filed it.'
uncertainty: No number of days. The erroneous-warrant procedure is not published on any DTF page found.
designImplication: For NY, release is automatic on full payment, but there is no stated delay. Pick a short, explicit game delay and mark it as invented.

claim: No DTF procedure or deadline for contesting a warrant filed in error was found. Tax Law 6 lists 'vacaturs' among the warrant-related records DTF must file. That shows a vacated warrant is recorded publicly, but not how a taxpayer obtains it.
sourceDate: Tax Law 6 as displayed by the NY Senate; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Tax Law 6 covers 'warrant satisfactions, vacaturs, amendments and expirations', which must be filed electronically without fees.
uncertainty: Secondary sources say DTF vacates warrants filed in error, but none of them is official.
designImplication: For NY, the game can model 'vacated' as a warrant status. The path to it is unsourced, so keep it a manual, rare event.

claim: A NY installment payment agreement does not withhold or release a warrant. DTF may file a warrant whether or not the taxpayer enters an agreement. Under an agreement, the warrant stays on file as a lien until the full warranted balance is paid. No rule found requires a warrant as a condition of an agreement.
establishes: Pub 131: 'Whether or not you enter into a payment agreement, we may also file a tax warrant with the New York State Department of State and in the appropriate New York State county clerk's office.' tax-warrants.htm: 'If you set up an IPA, the warrant will remain on file and continue to be a lien on your real and personal property until you pay your total warranted balance in full.' Pub 131: an agreement may be terminated or modified 'only upon at least 30 days prior notice' except in jeopardy.
uncertainty: None on the main point.
designImplication: In NY, an agreement stops other collection actions but not the warrant. Keep the lien flag on through the plan.

claim: NY warrants are public records. The Department of State must make warrants and warrant-related records searchable by name, and DTF offers its own warrant search. DTF names these effects: a warrant 'may affect your ... ability to buy or sell real property' and allows seizure and sale of property and wage garnishment.

value.searchable: by name, Department of State Tax Warrant Notice System; DTF warrant search
stateNamedEffects: may affect ability to buy or sell real property
allows seizure and sale of real and personal property
allows garnishment of wages or other income

sourceDate: DTF-996 (current form, undated in text read); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DTF-996: 'Warrants are public records filed with the Department of State and with your county clerk's office.' Tax Law 6: the Department of State must make warrant information 'available to the public and searchable by the name of the person or persons listed in the tax warrant.'
uncertainty: DTF also mentions a credit effect. Per instructions, that was not researched or recorded.
designImplication: For NY, a warrant should block or complicate property sales in the game. The other named effects are collection powers, not penalties.

claim: In CA a statutory lien arises automatically when income tax becomes due and payable and is unpaid (R&TC 19221). It attaches to all CA real and personal property. FTB then 'may' record or file a Notice of State Tax Lien if the taxpayer does not respond to its letters, pay in full or set up a payment plan. No minimum amount was found.

value.noticeFiledWhen: taxpayer does not respond to letters, pay in full, or set up a payment plan

establishes: FTB Liens page: 'When you owe tax debt, we automatically have a statutory lien that attaches to all California real or personal property you own or have rights to.' 'If you don't respond to our letters, pay in full, or set a payment plan, we may record and/or file a Notice of State Tax Lien against you.' FTB bill analysis of AB 2224 (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2025-2026/AB2224-021926.pdf): 'A state tax lien for unpaid state income taxes arises automatically and by operation of law when taxes become due and payable pursuant to Revenue and Taxation Code (RTC) section 19221.'
uncertainty: R&TC 19221 itself was not read. leginfo.legislature.ca.gov returned a bot challenge. The statement is FTB's.
designImplication: For CA, model two states: a silent statutory lien from the due date, and a recorded Notice of State Tax Lien later. Only the recorded one is public.

claim: At least 30 days before recording or filing a lien, FTB must mail a notice. It states the authority for the lien and the procedures available to prevent it. If within those 30 days the taxpayer shows that recording would be in error, the lien is not recorded. Separately, the taxpayer may request an independent administrative review within 30 days of the date of the Notice of State Tax Lien.

value.preFilingNoticeNameNote: NOT FOUND (the 30-day notice is described but not named)
value.preventionWithinNoticePeriod: prove the filing would be in error
value.postFilingReviewTrigger: date of the Notice of State Tax Lien

establishes: FTB 4058: 'At least 30 days prior to recording or filing a tax lien, we must mail you a notice stating by what authority we are filing the lien, and what procedures are available to you to prevent us from filing it. The lien will not be filed or recorded if, within the 30 days, you prove that such filing or recording would be in error.' FTB 1140 (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/misc/1140.html): 'You must submit your request for review within 30 days of the date of the Final Notice Before Levy or within 30 days of the date of the Notice of State Tax Lien.'
uncertainty: The pre-filing notice's form name is not given on the pages read.
designImplication: For CA, use a 30-day pre-lien notice with a 'show it's wrong' escape, then a 30-day review window after filing.

claim: FTB records a Notice of State Tax Lien with one or more county recorders for real property. It files one with the CA Secretary of State for personal property. FTB charges the taxpayer a 'lien fee' for filing and releasing. FTB lists the amount as varying by county. FTB's own bill analysis says the recording fee collected from the taxpayer is currently up to $10. If it is not collected at filing, FTB collects twice the first-page fee, up to $20, at release. AB 2224 would raise the first-page fee to a flat $15 from January 1, 2027, making the release fee up to $30.

pendingChange.status: bill under analysis; enactment NOT FOUND

sourceDate: FTB bill analysis of AB 2224, dated 2026-02-19 per filename; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: AB 2224 analysis: 'FTB records state tax liens with county recorders under GOV section 7171 and collects from the taxpayer the applicable recording fee, currently up to $10, at the time the lien is filed. If a recording fee is not collected from the taxpayer at the time the lien is filed, the FTB collects two times the recording fee for the first page of a lien, currently up to $20, when the FTB records the release of the lien.' FTB fees page (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/pay/penalties-and-interest/index.html): 'Lien fee ... In-state: Varies county-to-county Out-of-state: Varies'.
uncertainty: Whether AB 2224 passed was not checked. The Secretary of State filing fee was not found.
designImplication: For CA, charge a small lien fee of up to $10 at filing, or up to $20 at release if none was collected. It is a real cost to the taxpayer.

claim: A recorded or filed CA Notice of State Tax Lien attaches to any CA real or personal property the taxpayer owns now or acquires later. It lasts 10 years from recording or filing, and FTB may extend it by sending and recording a new notice. FTB does not release an expired lien.

value.attachesTo: all CA real and personal property, current and after-acquired
value.extensionMethod: new Notice of State Tax Lien recorded/filed

establishes: FTB Help with liens: 'A lien expires 10 years from the date of recording or filing, unless we extend it. If we extend the lien, we will send a new Notice of State Tax Lien and record or file it with the county recorder or California Secretary of State. We will not release expired liens.' FTB Liens page: the lien 'Attaches to any California real or personal property you currently own or may acquire in the future' and 'Is effective for at least 10 years (may be extended)'.
uncertainty: The extension limit (how many times) is not stated on FTB pages. Gov Code 7172 was not read directly.
designImplication: For CA, use a ten-year lien that FTB can renew. Expiry ends it without any release document.

claim: After full payment of the liened years (tax, penalties, interest and fees), FTB starts the release once the payment posts, without a request. Government Code 7174 requires a certificate of release within 40 days after the liability is satisfied. If payment is by check, the 40 days start when the check clears. A release may cost up to $20 if the recording fee was not collected at filing. If FTB finds a lien was filed in error, it releases it with the county recorder or Secretary of State and says so.

value.checkRule: 40 days run from when the check is paid by the bank
value.releaseFee: up to $20 if the recording fee was not collected at filing
value.erroneousFiling: FTB releases it and issues a release stating it was filed in error

establishes: FTB Liens page: 'The quickest way we will release a Notice of State Tax Lien is for you to pay your liened tax debt in full (including interest, penalties, and fees). We will begin the lien release process once the payment is posted.' FTB 4058: 'If we agree with you, we will send a release stating that the lien was filed in error.' The 40-day rule is Gov Code 7174(c). It was read only as a search-result summary of Justia and FindLaw (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-7174/) and a CDTFA manual (https://cdtfa.ca.gov/taxes-and-fees/manuals/CPPM-Ch7-Liens-Email.pdf).
uncertainty: The 40-day figure is weakly sourced. The statute text was not read directly because leginfo blocked automated access, and FTB's own pages read in this pass do not state a number of days.
designImplication: For CA, auto-release within 40 days of a cleared payment is a reasonable model. Mark the 40 days as statute-via-secondary.

claim: FTB treats a lien as filed in error only if the balance was resolved before the recording date. That means paid in full, or a refund, zero-balance or fully paid return filed. A lien filed in violation of FTB's administrative procedures, or of an installment agreement in good standing, must be released as though filed in error. The taxpayer calls or writes FTB. The deadlines are the 30-day pre-filing window and a 30-day administrative review after the Notice of State Tax Lien. No deadline was found for FTB to act on the claim.

definitionOfError: balance resolved before the lien recording date
filed in violation of FTB administrative procedures
filed in violation of an installment agreement in good standing

establishes: Help with liens: 'Sometimes there is a mistake and a lien is filed against you in error. For example, the balance was resolved before the lien recording date ... If these were resolved after the lien recording date, the lien is not considered to be "filed in error."' FTB 4058: 'If we file or record a lien in violation of our administrative procedures or in violation of the terms of an installment agreement, we must release the lien as though we filed or recorded it in error.'
uncertainty: None on the definition. No response deadline was found.
designImplication: For CA, 'error' should be testable: was the balance zero before the recording date, or was a plan in good standing? Do not let paying afterwards count as error.

claim: Filing a lien against a liability covered by an installment agreement in good standing is an FTB error, unless the agreement allows it. So a current plan withholds new liens. FTB may still require a lien as a condition of approving a plan. Plans over $25,000 or longer than 60 months get periodic review. FTB says it may file a lien to protect the state until the liability is paid.
establishes: Terms and conditions: 'We may file a lien and/or request a financial statement as a condition for approval.' 'We may file a state tax lien to protect the state's interest until you pay off your tax liability (Government Code Sections 7170-7173).' 'If your tax liability exceeds $25,000, or the payment plan period of payment exceeds 60 months, or both, your payment plan agreement is subject to periodic review.' FTB 4058: 'We are also in error if you have an installment agreement in good standing with us to satisfy the tax liability for which we are issuing the levy or filing the lien, unless the levy is allowed by agreement.'
uncertainty: The two FTB statements fit together only if a lien filed as a condition of approval is 'allowed by agreement'. That reading is inferred. That an existing lien stays until payment is inferred from the release rule (full payment), not stated for plans.
designImplication: For CA, a lien may come with plan approval. After approval, no new lien while the plan is in good standing.

claim: Once recorded or filed, a CA Notice of State Tax Lien becomes public record. FTB names these effects: the taxpayer may be unable to buy, sell, refinance or transfer property, get a personal or business loan, or get or keep a job. FTB says it does not report liens to credit bureaus itself.

stateNamedEffects: may not be able to buy, sell, refinance, or transfer property
may not be able to get a personal or business loan
may not be able to get or keep a job

establishes: FTB Liens page: 'Once a Notice of State Tax Lien is recorded or filed against you, the lien: Becomes public record ... When a lien becomes public record, you may not be able to: Buy, sell, refinance, or transfer property; Get a personal or business loan; Get or keep a job.'
uncertainty: These are 'may' effects named by FTB, not mechanics. Credit effects were deliberately not recorded.
designImplication: For CA, the public lien can gate property transactions and loans in the game. Treat the job effect as flavor unless a hiring system reads it.

claim: In AZ unpaid tax becomes a lien automatically on all of the taxpayer's property, real and personal, from the date it is assessed or the return is filed. It lasts until satisfied (ARS 42-1151(A)). The lien is not valid against purchasers, security-interest holders, mechanic's lienholders or judgment lien creditors until notice is recorded under 42-1152. No minimum amount or days-after-demand rule for recording was found.

value.arisesFrom: date assessed or date the return showing the liability is filed
value.attachesTo: all property and rights to property, real or personal, including after-acquired

sourceDate: ARS 42-1151 as published by the AZ Legislature; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ARS 42-1151(A): unpaid amounts 'constitute a lien upon all property and rights to property, whether real or personal, belonging to the taxpayer or acquired by the taxpayer from the date the amounts are assessed or the date the return prescribing the liability is filed until the liability for the assessed amounts is satisfied.'
uncertainty: ADOR's pages do not say when it decides to record a notice.
designImplication: For AZ, the lien exists from assessment. Recording is a separate, discretionary step that makes it bite against third parties.

claim: No statutory or ADOR-published notice of intent to record a lien was found for AZ. ARS 42-1152 sets out the content of the recorded notice but no advance notice to the taxpayer.
sourceDate: ARS 42-1152 as published by the AZ Legislature; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ARS 42-1152(C): the recorded notice 'shall specify the nature of the tax, the amount of tax, interest and penalty and other amounts owed ... the taxable periods for which such amounts are due and the name and last known address of the taxpayer'. No advance-notice requirement appears in 42-1151 to 42-1155.
uncertainty: ADOR may send billing notices before recording, but none naming a lien deadline was found.
designImplication: For AZ, do not invent a pre-lien warning period. Recording can follow the bill without a stated gap.

claim: ADOR records a notice of lien against real property with the county recorder of any county. It records against personal property with the Secretary of State. No recording fee charged to the taxpayer was found.
sourceDate: ARS 42-1152 as published by the AZ Legislature; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ARS 42-1152(A): notice 'may be filed by the department against the taxpayer's real property located in any county by recording a notice of lien ... in the office of the county recorder.' 42-1152(B): against personal property 'by recording a notice of lien ... in the office of the secretary of state.'
uncertainty: None on the offices. The fee is unknown.
designImplication: For AZ, use county recorder plus Secretary of State, with no fee to the taxpayer until one is sourced.

claim: The AZ lien attaches to all real and personal property and rights to property, including after-acquired property, until the liability is satisfied. No fixed expiry for the lien was found. The department may not bring a collection action more than ten years after the tax becomes final, unless extended by agreement or tolled by a stay.

value.attachesTo: all property and rights to property, real or personal, including after-acquired
value.extendable: by agreement, or tolled while collection is stayed

sourceDate: ARS 42-1114 as published by the AZ Legislature; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ARS 42-1114(C): 'The action shall not commence more than ten years after the amount of taxes determined to be due becomes final unless the taxpayer and the department extend the ten year limitation or enforced collection has been stayed by operation of federal or state law.'
uncertainty: Whether the lien itself dies at ten years is not stated. 42-1114(C) limits suits, and 42-1151 says the lien lasts until satisfied.
designImplication: For AZ, model the lien as lasting until paid, with a ten-year cap on enforcement.

claim: When an AZ lien is satisfied, ADOR must issue a release to the taxpayer and record it in each county where the lien was recorded, and with the Secretary of State if applicable (ARS 42-1153(C)). ADOR's page sets the timing by payment method. For cash, certified funds or online payment, a Notice of Intent to Release State Tax Lien is issued immediately or within 24 hours, and the full release posts in 2 to 3 weeks. For a personal check, the notice comes within 45 days and the release can take 60 days. No request is needed. No release fee was found. ADOR may withdraw a notice that was premature or otherwise filed against its procedures.

value.erroneousFiling: discretionary withdrawal if premature or against ADOR procedures (ARS 42-1153(B)(2))

establishes: ADOR Tax Liens for Individuals: 'Once a payment has posted online, a letter of Notice of Intent to Release State Tax Lien will be provided within 24 hours to the taxpayer. Please allow 2-3 weeks for the full release to post with the appropriate County Recorder's Office and/or Secretary of State.' 'Once a personal check has been posted, a Notice of Intent to Release Lien will be provided to the taxpayer within 45 days. Please allow 60 days after making a payment by personal check for the full release to post.' ARS 42-1153(C) (https://www.azleg.gov/ars/42/01153.htm): 'The department shall record the lien release in any county where the original lien was recorded and in the office of the secretary of state if applicable.'
uncertainty: The page tells taxpayers how to record a Certificate of Release themselves, which seems at odds with ADOR recording it under 42-1153(C). Both are recorded here.
designImplication: For AZ, auto-release about 2 to 3 weeks after an electronic payment, or 60 days after a personal check. The payment method sets the delay.

claim: AZ has no taxpayer-initiated procedure or deadline for an erroneous lien in the sources read. ARS 42-1153(B) lets ADOR, 'in its discretion and at any time', withdraw a recorded notice. One of the listed grounds is that filing it was premature or otherwise against ADOR's administrative procedures.

value.process: department discretion; no taxpayer procedure found
withdrawalGrounds: filing premature or in violation of administrative procedures
taxpayer entered an installment payment agreement, unless the agreement provides otherwise

sourceDate: ARS 42-1153 as published by the AZ Legislature; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ARS 42-1153(B): 'In its discretion and at any time, the department may withdraw a notice of lien that was recorded pursuant to this article if the department determines that any of the following conditions applies: ... 2. Filing the lien was premature or otherwise in violation of the department's administrative procedures.'
uncertainty: Withdrawal is discretionary ('may'), not a right.
designImplication: For AZ, an erroneous lien is fixed only if the department chooses to. Model it as a request with uncertain success.

claim: ADOR may withdraw a recorded lien notice when the taxpayer enters an installment payment agreement, unless the agreement provides otherwise (ARS 42-1153(B)(4)). This is discretionary. ADOR's payment-arrangement page says a lien may be filed depending on the amount owed and the length of time to repay. Missing plan terms can lead to a lien. No fixed amount or month threshold was found.

value.lienMayBeConditionOfPlan: depends on amount owed and repayment length

establishes: ADOR Payment Arrangement for Individuals: 'Depending upon the amount owed and the length of time it will take to repay a liability, a tax lien may be filed.' 'If the terms of the arrangements are not kept, the Department will consider enforcement action, such as the filing of a tax lien.' ARS 42-1153(B)(4): withdrawal if 'The taxpayer has entered into an installment payment agreement, unless the agreement provides otherwise.'
uncertainty: ADOR does not publish the amount or term that triggers a plan lien.
designImplication: For AZ, a large or long plan may come with a lien. A plan may also get an existing lien withdrawn. Both are discretionary, so tie them to plan size, not to a fixed rule.

claim: AZ liens are recorded with the county recorder and Secretary of State. The sources read do not name any effect of that recording beyond its validity against later purchasers, security-interest holders and judgment creditors.

value.publicBasis: county recorder / Secretary of State recording
value.stateNamedEffect: lien becomes valid against purchasers, security holders, mechanic's lienholders and judgment lien creditors

sourceDate: ARS 42-1151 as published by the AZ Legislature; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ARS 42-1151(B): the lien 'is not valid against the following until the notice of the lien is filed as prescribed in section 42-1152', listing purchasers, security-interest holders, mechanic's lienholders and judgment lien creditors.
uncertainty: That recorder records are public is general law, not an ADOR statement.
designImplication: For AZ, the effect of recording is priority. Recording should matter when the player sells or borrows.

claim: For CO, the trigger found is the Notice of Intent to Issue Judgment/Lien. CDOR sends it to the last known address, and the taxpayer then has 10 days to pay in full with certified funds. Under CRS 39-21-114(3), a copy of the distraint warrant is filed with the district court clerk, who enters a judgment. A transcript of it, filed with a county clerk and recorder, becomes a lien on real property. No minimum amount was found.

value.noticeName: Notice of Intent to Issue Judgment/Lien
value.payWith: certified funds (bank cashier's check or money order)
value.mechanism: warrant docketed as a judgment by the district court clerk; transcript filed with a county clerk and recorder

establishes: CDOR Collections: 'CDOR will send a Notice of Intent to Issue Judgment/Lien to the taxpayer's last known address' and 'the taxpayer has 10 days from the date of the notice to pay the balance in full with certified funds.' 'Only a bank cashier's check or a money order can be accepted as certified funds.'
uncertainty: CRS 39-21-114 was read on FindLaw (https://codes.findlaw.com/co/title-39-taxation/co-rev-st-sect-39-21-114/), a secondary host. Justia and the official site were not reachable.
designImplication: For CO, use one 10-day notice before the judgment/lien. Only certified funds stop it, so an ordinary payment in the window should not count.

claim: The CO notice before a lien is the Notice of Intent to Issue Judgment/Lien. It gives 10 days from the date of the notice to pay the balance in full with certified funds. No form number was found.

value.noticeName: Notice of Intent to Issue Judgment/Lien

establishes: CDOR Collections: 'the taxpayer has 10 days from the date of the notice to pay the balance in full with certified funds.'
uncertainty: None on name and days.
designImplication: For CO, the 10-day notice is the shortest fuse in this set of states.

claim: A CO judgment becomes a real-property lien when its transcript is filed with a county clerk and recorder. A personal-property lien arises when a notice of lien is filed with the person holding the property. CO state tax liens are not filed with the Secretary of State. No recording fee charged to the taxpayer for the filing was found.

value.realPropertyOffice: county clerk and recorder (transcript of judgment entered by district court clerk)
value.personalPropertyMethod: notice of lien filed with the person in possession of the property (CRS 39-21-114(4))

establishes: CO Secretary of State FAQ: 'Colorado state tax liens are filed with the Colorado Department of Revenue's Division of Taxation.' CRS 39-21-114(3) (FindLaw): the transcript 'may be filed with the clerk and recorder of any county, and, from the time of such filing, such judgment shall become a lien upon all the real property'. 39-21-114(4): a notice of lien filed with a person in possession of personal property 'shall operate as a lien upon such personal property ... from the date of such filing.'
uncertainty: The statute text is from a secondary host. The SOS wording that liens are filed 'with the Department of Revenue' is odd. County recording per the statute is what governs real property.
designImplication: For CO, real-property liens are per county. A personal-property lien is served on whoever holds the asset, which is close to a levy.

claim: A CO judgment lien attaches to all of the taxpayer's real property in each county where the transcript is filed. CDOR says it attaches to all assets 'such as property and vehicles'. It lasts six years from entry of the judgment unless satisfied earlier. No renewal provision was confirmed.

value.attachesTo: real property in each county where the transcript is filed; CDOR says 'all of your assets (such as property and vehicles)'

sourceDate: CRS 39-21-114 as displayed by FindLaw; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: CRS 39-21-114(3): 'The lien shall continue for six years from the entry of the judgment unless the judgment is previously satisfied.' CDOR Collections: 'Once filed, a judgment/lien attaches to all of your assets (such as property and vehicles) and will prevent you from selling them without first paying your tax debt.'
uncertainty: The statute was read on a secondary host. A renewal clause may exist in the omitted text.
designImplication: For CO, use a six-year lien, the shortest in this set.

claim: When a CO lien is fully satisfied, CDOR issues a Release of Lien that directs the county clerk to enter satisfaction. The document tells the taxpayer to file it with the county Clerk and Recorder: 'You must file this release'. No release deadline in days was found. No CDOR release fee was found. Any county recording fee for the release is not quantified here. No erroneous-filing release procedure was found.
sourceDate: example CDOR release dated Mar 24, 2022, hosted by Arapahoe County; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: CDOR Release of Lien (example): the claim of lien 'has been fully satisfied and said claim of lien is hereby released ... I hereby authorize and direct the clerk of said County to enter of record satisfaction of said lien/judgment in said action.' 'NOTE: You must file this release with the Clerk and Recorder of the above county.'
uncertainty: The document is a CDOR form, but hosted by a county as an example, not by CDOR. It is official in origin and secondary in hosting.
designImplication: For CO, as in CT, the player must take the release and record it. Releases are not automatic.

claim: No CDOR or statutory procedure or deadline was found for disputing a CO lien filed in error.
establishes: The CDOR Collections page and CRS 39-21-114 (FindLaw) were read. Neither covers an erroneous lien.
uncertainty: Not researched beyond those sources and one search.
designImplication: Leave CO erroneous-lien handling unmodelled.

claim: CDOR's payment-plan pages do not mention liens. Standard plans for non-business accounts run up to 36 months, and a signed agreement waives the collection statute of limitations. A plan cannot be requested if the debt is with a collection agency or under a wage levy. Whether a lien is withheld or released during a plan, or required for one, was not found on an official page.
establishes: CDOR Payment Plans: 'Standard payment plans typically allow for a maximum of 36 months for non-business accounts.' The waiver of the collection statute of limitations comes from a search-result summary of tax.colorado.gov pages, not from a page read directly.
uncertainty: The waiver is weakly sourced. A secondary source (gettaxreliefnow.com) says the state may keep a lien in place during a plan. That is not used.
designImplication: For CO, keep lien and plan independent until an official source links them.

claim: A CO judgment lien is recorded with the county clerk and recorder. CDOR names one effect: a filed judgment/lien 'will prevent you from selling' your assets 'without first paying your tax debt.'

value.publicBasis: county clerk and recorder records; court judgment docket
stateNamedEffects: prevents selling assets (such as property and vehicles) without first paying the tax debt

establishes: CDOR Collections: 'Once filed, a judgment/lien attaches to all of your assets (such as property and vehicles) and will prevent you from selling them without first paying your tax debt.'
uncertainty: That the records are public is general law.
designImplication: For CO, a lien should block asset sales until paid. That is a concrete, testable effect.

claim: In GA the lien is the state tax execution, also called a fi. fa. For individual income tax, the lien arises and attaches only when a tax execution is filed with the clerk of superior court (OCGA 48-2-56(e)). It must be recorded within 5 years of the assessment date. The execution follows the Official Assessment and Demand for Payment. DOR says that once a liability is due and in collection it 'may file a lien without notice, at any time'. No minimum amount was found.

value.arisesWhen: tax execution filed with the clerk of superior court
value.precedingNotice: Official Assessment and Demand for Payment

establishes: GA DOR Liens: 'After a tax liability has become due and is in the collection process, the Department may file a lien without notice, at any time, if it is in the state's best interest.' 'State tax liens must be recorded within 5 years of the assessment date.' OCGA 48-2-56 (FindLaw, https://codes.findlaw.com/ga/title-48-revenue-and-taxation/ga-code-sect-48-2-56/): income tax liens 'arise and attach to all property of the taxpayer as of the time a tax execution for these taxes is filed with the clerk of superior court'.
uncertainty: OCGA was read on FindLaw, a secondary host.
designImplication: For GA, the lien exists only once filed. Allow filing any time after the assessment is final, without a separate warning.

claim: GA has no lien-specific notice of intent. DOR says it 'may file a lien without notice' once a liability is due and in collection. The notices before it are the Proposed Assessment, which gives 45 days to pay or protest, and the Official Assessment and Demand for Payment, which gives 45 more days to appeal to the Tax Court or superior court. After a lien is issued, a Notice of State Tax Execution letter informs the taxpayer.

precedingNotices.name: Official Assessment and Demand for Payment

establishes: GA DOR Official Assessment letter page: 'You had 45 days from the date on the Proposed Assessment Letter to: Pay the amount due, or protest the amount due.' 'If you disagree or dispute the amount owed or the tax due, then you still have 45 additional calendar days to file an appeal with the Georgia Tax Court or with your local Superior Court.' 'DOR may issue and record a tax lien with the Clerk of Superior Court.'
uncertainty: Whether DOR waits out the 45-day appeal window before filing is implied, not stated.
designImplication: For GA, the warnings are the assessment notices. The lien itself can come unannounced.

claim: GA state tax executions are recorded with one or more Clerks of Superior Court, through the GSCCCA statewide system (SOLVED). For real property, an execution must be filed in the county where the property lies. Issuing a tax execution adds a 20% collection fee to the liability. No clerk recording fee charged to the taxpayer was found.

value.office: Clerk of Superior Court (one or more counties)
value.realPropertyRule: execution must be filed in the county where the real property is located

establishes: GA-9465 instructions: 'The issuance of a tax execution will result in the imposition of an additional 20% collection fee that will be added to the tax liability.' GA DOR Liens (https://dor.georgia.gov/liens): a state tax lien 'is recorded with one or more Clerks of Superior Court to make it a matter of public record and to secure the debt.' OCGA 48-2-56(e) (FindLaw): 'Before the lien ... shall attach to real property, an execution shall be filed with the clerk of superior court in the county where the real property is located.'
uncertainty: The 20% fee is stated in a form's instructions. The statute imposing it was not read.
designImplication: For GA, a lien costs the player 20% of the liability at once. That is the biggest lien-triggered charge in this set.

claim: A GA state tax execution attaches to any property the named taxpayer owns of record when it becomes active. It stays attached through a change of ownership, and on a sale it attaches to the proportionate proceeds. After recording, DOR has 10 years to collect. Bankruptcy, installment agreements, offers in compromise and appeals extend that, and the lien cannot be renewed. Expired, statute-barred liens are released.

value.attachesTo: any property of record owned by the named taxpayer when the lien becomes active

establishes: GA DOR Lien FAQ: 'After the Department records a state tax execution, they have 10 years from the recording date to collect the tax liability.' 'State tax liens may not be renewed.' GA DOR Liens: 'If ownership of the subject property changes, the Department's lien remains attached until the lien is resolved. When there is a sale of the subject property, the lien attaches to the proportionate proceeds from the sale.'
uncertainty: The extension list is from the FAQ as summarized. The exact tolling arithmetic is not given.
designImplication: For GA, the lien lasts ten years and is not renewable. A payment plan extends the clock, so long plans keep the lien alive longer.

claim: GA DOR releases a lien within five days after full payment posts to the taxpayer's account. It files the release electronically with the Clerk of Superior Court in each county where the lien was recorded. No taxpayer request is needed. No release fee was found. If DOR finds a lien was recorded in error, it withdraws it by amending the lien to state that it has been officially withdrawn. Expired liens are also released.

value.from: full payment posts to the account
value.erroneousFiling: lien withdrawn; amended to state it is officially withdrawn

establishes: GA DOR Lien FAQ: 'The Department will release a lien within five days after the full payment posts to the taxpayer's account.' GA DOR Liens: 'The Department will electronically submit a lien release with the Clerk of Superior Court in each county where the lien had been recorded.' 'If the Department recorded a state tax lien against you in error, the Department would amend the lien by stating that it has been officially withdrawn.'
uncertainty: The statute (OCGA 48-3-28, via FindLaw) says only 'as soon as reasonably possible'. The five days is DOR's own commitment.
designImplication: For GA, auto-release five days after the payment posts.

claim: GA DOR withdraws a lien it finds was filed in error and amends it to show official withdrawal. No taxpayer procedure, form or deadline for raising the error was found.

value.process: contact DOR; withdrawal on DOR determination

establishes: GA DOR Liens: 'Withdrawal If the Department determines that the lien was filed in error, the lien will be withdrawn.'
uncertainty: None beyond the missing procedure.
designImplication: For GA, 'withdrawn in error' is a lien end state, distinct from 'released after payment'.

claim: A GA installment agreement does not release an existing lien, which must be paid in full. If an execution was already recorded before approval, DOR will not start enforcement while the agreement holds. Default allows all enforced collection, including filing an execution. Agreements run up to 60 months with a $25 minimum monthly payment and a $50 administration fee. That fee is $25 if income is under $22,050, and $100 for paper-check plans. No source found says a plan requires a lien.
establishes: GA-9465: 'If a tax execution has already been recorded prior to the approval of the agreement, the Department will not initiate enforcement action against you to collect the outstanding tax debt. Upon default of the installment agreement, the Department may initiate all appropriate enforced collection activity.' GA DOR Lien FAQ: 'The tax lien must be paid in full for the lien to be released.' GA DOR Payment Plans (https://dor.georgia.gov/payment-plans): 'The installment payment agreement cannot exceed 60 months'; 'The minimum monthly payment is $25.'
uncertainty: A search summary said an agreement 'stops new liens'. That wording was not found on the official pages read, so it is not asserted.
designImplication: For GA, a plan freezes enforcement on an existing lien but keeps the lien. Default re-arms everything.

claim: A recorded GA tax lien makes the tax debt public record and is searchable through SOLVED in the Georgia Tax Center. DOR names its effects: the lien 'may hamper the transfer of real or personal property', and 'will block the transfer of title of any other properties owned or later acquired'. DOR says it does not report liens to credit agencies.

value.searchable: Georgia Tax Center, 'SOLVED: Search for a Lien'
stateNamedEffects: may hamper the transfer of real or personal property
blocks transfer of title of other properties owned or later acquired (after a partial release)
allows the Department to initiate collection enforcement actions

establishes: GA DOR Lien FAQ: 'When a tax lien is recorded your tax debt become public record.' A tax lien 'may hamper the transfer of real or personal property.' 'A tax lien filed with the Superior Court makes your tax debt public record and allows the Department to initiate collection enforcement actions.'
uncertainty: None.
designImplication: For GA, a lien should block property transfer, and it is visible to anyone who searches.

claim: In HI the lien arises automatically and attaches to all property and rights to property. It arises at whichever comes first: assessment, filing of the return, or the department's recording of a lien certificate (HRS 231-33(b)). Until a certificate is recorded, it is not valid against prior mortgagees, purchasers or judgment creditors of real property. The department may record a certificate for taxes returned, assessed, or under a notice of proposed assessment. No minimum amount was found.

value.certificateMayCover: taxes returned, assessed, or under a notice of proposed assessment

sourceDate: HRS ch. 231, unofficial DOTAX compilation as of 12/31/2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: HRS 231-33(b): 'The lien for the tax, including penalties and interest thereon, arises at the time the tax is assessed, or at the time a return thereof is filed, or at the time of filing by the department of taxation of the certificate provided for by subsection (f) whichever first occurs.' 231-33(f): the department 'may record in the bureau of conveyances at Honolulu ... a certificate setting forth the amount of taxes due and unpaid, which have been returned, assessed, or as to which a notice of proposed assessment has issued.'
uncertainty: From January 1, 2027 the certificate must also state the assessment date (L 2025, c 68).
designImplication: For HI, the lien exists from assessment or filing. Recording can come even before the assessment is final.

claim: No HI notice of intent specifically before a lien was found. The collection-fee rule requires a written notice demanding payment and warning of collection action, with a deadline at least 10 calendar days after mailing. That governs when collection fees, including the lien recording fee, may be charged. It does not govern when a lien may be recorded.

feeNotice.content: demand for payment; warns that continued failure may result in collection action and fees

sourceDate: HAR ch. 18-231, unofficial DOTAX compilation as of 12/31/2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: HAR 18-231-25.5-02(c): 'Fees imposed under this section may be charged after the department has mailed written notice to a taxpayer demanding payment of delinquent taxes and advising that continued failure to pay the amount due may result in collection action, including the imposition of fees under this section.' (d): the notice 'shall contain a deadline date, no earlier than ten calendar days after the date of mailing, before which no fee set forth in this section may be charged.'
uncertainty: The case note to HRS 231-33 records that a pre-hearing tax lien does not violate due process (57 H. 1 (1976)). That suggests no pre-lien hearing is required.
designImplication: For HI, use a 10-day demand notice before fees can be charged. Lien recording itself needs no separate warning.

claim: HI records lien certificates in the Bureau of Conveyances at Honolulu, and files them with the county director of finance for motor vehicles. Recording in the Bureau also makes it a lien on Land Court registered land. The taxpayer is charged $25 for recording a certificate of tax lien and $25 for recording its release at the Bureau, plus any other recording fees the department incurs. Any filing cost becomes part of the lien.
sourceDate: HAR ch. 18-231, unofficial DOTAX compilation as of 12/31/2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: HAR 18-231-25.5-02(f)(5): 'For recording a certificate of tax lien or a release of tax lien, $25 for recording at the Bureau of Conveyances, plus any other recording fees that are actually charged to and incurred by the department for recording with other agencies (such as with a county director of finance).' HRS 231-33(f): 'Any cost incurred in the filing of the certificate shall be a part of the lien for the tax therein set forth.'
uncertainty: Fees may be waived for hardship (HAR 18-231-25.5-01(b)).
designImplication: For HI, charge $25 at recording and $25 at release, posted to the tax account as fees.

claim: The HI lien attaches to all property and rights to property, real and personal, of the person liable. Once it arises it is 'paramount' against all parties, with the exceptions in 231-33(c) to (e). No fixed lien expiry was found. Income tax must be collected by levy or court proceeding within fifteen years after assessment, and a payment plan voluntarily extends that period. If a recorded lien draws no response for 365 days, the director may ask the circuit court to convert it into a civil judgment.

value.attachesTo: all property and rights to property, real or personal

sourceDate: HRS ch. 235, unofficial DOTAX compilation as of 12/31/2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: HRS 235-111: 'the tax may be collected by levy or by a proceeding in court under chapter 231; provided that the levy is made or the proceeding was begun within fifteen years after the assessment of the tax.' HRS 231-33(j) (https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/legal/hrs/hrs_231.pdf): after 'three hundred sixty-five days have elapsed from the date of recording with no response or action by the taxpayer ... the director may apply to the circuit court to have the lien converted into a civil judgment.'
uncertainty: From 2027, 231-33(g) requires a discharge when the liability becomes unenforceable under 235-111. That implies the lien ends with the 15-year limit.
designImplication: For HI, the lien lasts until paid or until the 15-year limit. An ignored lien can become a court judgment after a year.

claim: HI satisfaction and release require payment of tax, penalties and interest, plus the release recording fee ($25 at the Bureau of Conveyances) and any other fee caused by the taxpayer. No number of days after payment was found, and no statement on whether the taxpayer must ask. From January 1, 2027, HRS 231-33(g) requires the department to issue a certificate of discharge for any liability that has been satisfied or become unenforceable. No erroneous-filing release procedure was found.
sourceDate: HRS ch. 231, unofficial DOTAX compilation as of 12/31/2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: HRS 231-33(g) (effective January 1, 2027): 'The department shall issue a certificate of discharge as to any liability that has been satisfied or that has become unenforceable under section 235-111.' HAR 18-231-25.5-02(f)(5): '$25 for recording ... a release of tax lien'.
uncertainty: A search summary quoted a rule that satisfaction includes 'recording fees at the current rate established by the Bureau of Conveyances'. That exact text was not located in the compilation, so the $25 HAR fee is used. Before 2027, discharge is discretionary ('may').
designImplication: For HI, charge the player $25 at release. Before 2027 the release is discretionary; from 2027 it is mandatory on satisfaction.

claim: No HI procedure or deadline for disputing a lien filed in error was found in the HRS or HAR chapter 231 compilations or on DOTAX collection pages.
sourceDate: HRS ch. 231, unofficial DOTAX compilation as of 12/31/2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: HRS 231-33 covers arising, priority, recording, discharge, foreclosure and conversion to judgment, but no erroneous-lien procedure.
uncertainty: The DOTAX Taxpayer Advocate or other pages were not searched exhaustively.
designImplication: Leave HI erroneous-lien handling unmodelled.

claim: In HI, a state tax lien 'will be initiated' to enter an installment plan agreement of more than one year. The department weighs the balance, the circumstances of noncompliance, compliance history and other facts. Plans over 12 months also need Form CM-2. A plan extends the collection limitation period. Default can bring a lien, levy, garnishment or referral. Plans carry a non-refundable $50 processing fee. No source says an existing lien is released during a plan.

value.lienRequirementWording: 'will be initiated' for plans longer than one year, considering balance, circumstances, compliance history

establishes: DOTAX Payment Plans: 'A state tax lien will be initiated to enter in an installment plan agreement for more than one year considering the amount of your balance due, nature of the circumstances that led to noncompliance, taxpayer's compliance history, and all other relevant facts necessary to protect the State's interest.' Form D-100 (https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/forms/2024/d100_i.pdf): 'If your installment plan will be longer than 12 months, please submit a Statement of Financial Condition, Form CM-2'; 'A non-refundable $50 processing fee may be assessed'.
uncertainty: 'Considering' the listed factors makes it unclear whether the lien is automatic for every plan over 12 months or only for some.
designImplication: For HI, a plan longer than 12 months brings a lien, and a 12-month plan does not. This is a clean threshold for the game.

claim: HI lien certificates are recorded in the Bureau of Conveyances, whose records are public. The statute names the effects: the lien becomes 'paramount' and valid against later mortgagees, purchasers and judgment creditors of real property, and it reaches Land Court registered land. An unanswered lien can become a civil judgment after 365 days.

stateNamedEffects: valid against later mortgagees, purchasers and judgment creditors of real property
procures a lien on Land Court registered land
may be converted to a civil judgment after 365 days of no response

sourceDate: HRS ch. 231, unofficial DOTAX compilation as of 12/31/2025; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: HRS 231-33(f): 'Recordation of the certificate in the bureau of conveyances shall be deemed, at such time, for all purposes and without any further action, to procure a lien on land registered in the land court under chapter 501.'
uncertainty: That Bureau records are public is general law, not stated by DOTAX in the sources read.
designImplication: For HI, the public lien should matter for property deals. Ignoring it for a year escalates it to a judgment.

claim: In IL a lien arises at assessment once a person 'neglects or refuses to pay ... after demand' (35 ILCS 5/1101(a)-(b)). It must be perfected by filing a notice in the State Tax Lien Registry. The notice must be filed within 3 years after the liability becomes final, or after an unpaid return was filed, or the lien terminates. For a deficiency, no notice may be filed until court review ends or the time for it runs out. That 3-year clock does not run during a repayment plan the taxpayer is complying with. No minimum amount was found.

value.condition: neglect or refusal to pay after demand
value.perfectedBy: notice of tax lien filed in the State Tax Lien Registry
value.from: final liability (end of review) or the filing of an unpaid return

sourceDate: 35 ILCS 5/1101 as amended by P.A. 104-468 (eff. 6-16-26); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 35 ILCS 5/1101(a): 'If any person liable to pay any tax neglects or refuses to pay the same after demand, the amount ... shall be a lien in favor of the State of Illinois upon all property and rights to property.' 1101(d): 'The lien created by assessment shall terminate unless a notice of lien is filed ... within 3 years.' 'The time limitation period on the Department's right to file a notice of lien shall not run ... (2) during the term of a repayment plan that taxpayer has entered into with the Department, as long as taxpayer remains in compliance.' 35 ILCS 750/1-15(a): 'the Department may file in the registry a notice of tax lien within 3 years from the date of the final tax liability.'
uncertainty: The repayment-plan tolling clause is new (eff. June 16, 2026).
designImplication: For IL, the lien needs a demand, then a registry filing within three years. A compliant plan pauses that three-year clock.

claim: No IL notice of intent specifically before a regular lien filing was found. 35 ILCS 5/1101 requires a 'demand' before the lien. IDOR's collection page describes a first bill but no pre-lien warning. Jeopardy liens differ. The taxpayer gets 5 days after the jeopardy notice to comply or show error, and 20 days after being told of the filing to protest.

value.regularLienNoticeNote: NOT FOUND (statute requires 'demand'; no named pre-lien notice)

establishes: 35 ILCS 5/1102(a)(2): 'If the taxpayer, within 5 days after such notice ... does not comply with such notice or show to the Department that the findings in such notice are erroneous, the Department may file a notice of jeopardy assessment lien'. 1102(c): the taxpayer 'may protest within 20 days after being notified by the Department of the filing of such jeopardy assessment lien'.
uncertainty: IDOR may send a lien-warning letter in practice. None appeared on the letters or collection pages read.
designImplication: For IL, the bill is the demand. Do not add a separate pre-lien notice for ordinary liens.

claim: Since January 1, 2018, IL liens are filed in the State Tax Lien Registry, a statewide public database that IDOR maintains. The registry supersedes county records. Liens filed with county recorders before 2018 stay valid. The taxpayer is liable for IDOR's filing fee for the lien and its filing fee for the release, and both must be paid before release. The fee amounts were not found.
establishes: 35 ILCS 5/1103(e): 'The taxpayer is liable for any filing fees imposed by the Department for filing the lien in the State Tax Lien Registry and any filing fees imposed by the Department for the release of that lien. The filing fees shall be paid to the Department in addition to payment of the tax, penalty, and interest.' 35 ILCS 750/1-25(b) (https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ILCS/details?ActID=3793&ChapterID=8): 'the registry shall supersede the records of any county.'
uncertainty: The only fees in 86 Ill. Adm. Code 720 are registry subscription fees ($500 new, $50 renewal). These are for data buyers, not lien fees.
designImplication: For IL, filing and release fees exist and gate the release, but their amount is unknown. Leave them as parameters.

claim: An IL registry lien attaches to all existing and after-acquired personal property, tangible and intangible, anywhere in IL. It attaches to real property only in the county or counties named in the notice. It lasts 20 years from filing unless released earlier. Interest and penalty keep accruing on the lien.

value.realProperty: only in the counties named in the notice

sourceDate: 35 ILCS 750 (State Tax Lien Registration Act); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 35 ILCS 750/1-25(a): 'A notice of tax lien shall be a lien upon the debtor's personal property, both tangible and intangible, located anywhere in the State, and a lien upon the real property of the debtor located in the county or counties as specified in the notice of tax lien, for a period of 20 years from the date of filing unless it is sooner released by the Department.' 35 ILCS 5/1104 agrees on 20 years.
uncertainty: None.
designImplication: For IL, a lien lasts 20 years. Real property is affected county by county, so a player's property in an unnamed county is free of it.

claim: After an IL liability is paid, IDOR releases the lien and files the release in the registry once the taxpayer has also paid the filing fees for the lien and the release. A release in the registry releases the lien in IDOR's records, the registry and the county. No deadline in days was found. The taxpayer contacts the Lien Unit for a release or payoff. IDOR says that if it issues a lien in error, it will issue a release.

value.taxpayerMustRequest: contact the Lien Unit for a release or payoff (IDOR page)
value.erroneousFiling: IDOR issues a release; taxpayer still liable for filing fees if a court finds nonliability (5/1105(b))

establishes: 35 ILCS 5/1105(a): 'Upon payment by the taxpayer to the Department in cash or by guaranteed remittance of an amount representing the filing fees and charges for the lien and the filing fees and charges for the release of that lien, the Department shall release all or any portion of the property subject to any lien ... and file that complete or partial release of lien in the State Tax Lien Registry'. IDOR Collection Process (https://tax.illinois.gov/individuals/collection.html): 'You will also be responsible for paying any applicable filing and release fees associated with the lien before the department will release the lien.' 'If we issue a lien in error, we will issue a release.'
uncertainty: 5/1105(b) makes the taxpayer pay filing fees even after a court finds no liability. That applies to a judicial finding, not to an IDOR-admitted error, where fee treatment is NOT FOUND.
designImplication: For IL, release needs full payment plus the fees. Model it as a request through the Lien Unit.

claim: IDOR states it will issue a release if it issues a lien in error. No procedure or deadline was found. On judicial review, if the court finds no liability or no jeopardy, the lien must be released to that extent, but the taxpayer still owes the filing and release fees. A jeopardy lien may be protested within 20 days of notice of filing.

value.process: contact IDOR Lien Unit; judicial review; jeopardy protest

establishes: IDOR: 'If we issue a lien in error, we will issue a release.' 35 ILCS 5/1105(b) (https://www.ilga.gov/Documents/legislation/ilcs/documents/003500050K1105.htm): 'The taxpayer shall, however, be liable for the filing fee imposed by the Department to file the lien and the filing fee imposed to release the lien.'
uncertainty: No timeline.
designImplication: For IL, even a lien beaten in court costs the taxpayer the fees. That is unusual and worth preserving.

claim: In IL, from June 16, 2026, the 3-year deadline for IDOR to file a notice of lien does not run while the taxpayer complies with a repayment plan. That implies IDOR may hold off filing during a compliant plan without losing the right. No source says a plan requires a lien or releases an existing one. The Taxpayers' Bill of Rights bars IDOR from cancelling an installment contract except for inaccurate financial information, an unpaid tax, or a non-response.

value.lienWithheldNote: NOT FOUND as an express rule (tolling implies deferral is possible)
planCancellationLimitedTo: no response to Department request for financial information

sourceDate: 35 ILCS 5/1101 as amended by P.A. 104-468 (eff. 6-16-26); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 35 ILCS 5/1101(d): the period 'shall not run ... (2) during the term of a repayment plan that taxpayer has entered into with the Department, as long as taxpayer remains in compliance with the terms of the repayment plan.' 20 ILCS 2520/4(d) (https://www.ilga.gov/Documents/legislation/ilcs/documents/002025200K4.htm): 'To not cancel any installment contracts unless the taxpayer fails to provide accurate financial information, fails to pay any tax or does not respond to any Department request for additional financial information.'
uncertainty: The deferral is an inference from the tolling clause, not a stated policy.
designImplication: For IL, a compliant plan pauses the lien-filing clock. If the plan fails, IDOR can still file.

claim: The IL State Tax Lien Registry is public and searchable by debtor name or lien number at no charge. Its data may be sold in bulk, but not for survey, marketing or solicitation. IDOR names these effects: in most cases the taxpayer cannot sell or transfer the property until the past-due amount is paid, and the lien is enforceable for 20 years.

value.searchable: by debtor name or tax lien number, free
stateNamedEffects: in most cases cannot sell or transfer the property until paid

establishes: IDOR Collection Process: 'If we file a lien on your real estate or personal property, in most cases you cannot sell or transfer your property until you pay your past-due amount.' 35 ILCS 750/1-30(b): 'Information in the registry shall be searchable by name of debtor or by tax lien number. The Department shall not charge for access to information in the registry.'
uncertainty: IDOR's page also names a credit effect. Per instructions, it was not recorded.
designImplication: For IL, a lien should block sale or transfer of the affected property until paid.

claim: In IN the lien is a tax warrant docketed as a judgment. If a liability is not paid or protested within 60 days of the first notice, DOR issues a Demand Notice. If the taxpayer does not pay or show reasonable cause within 20 days of its mailing, DOR may issue a warrant (IC 6-8.1-8-2(b)). Issuing it adds a 10% collection fee on the unpaid tax. The warrant may not be filed with a circuit court clerk until at least 20 days after the demand was mailed. When the clerk records it, it becomes a judgment and lien. No minimum amount was found.

value.lienCreatedWhen: clerk records the warrant in the judgment record

sourceDate: IC 6-8.1-8-2 as displayed by FindLaw, last updated January 1, 2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IC 6-8.1-8-2(b): 'If the person does not pay the amount demanded or show reasonable cause for not paying the amount demanded within the twenty (20) day period, the department may issue a tax warrant ... When the department issues a tax warrant, a collection fee of ten percent (10%) of the unpaid tax is added to the total amount due.' (c): it 'may not file the warrant with the circuit court clerk of any county in which the person owns property until at least twenty (20) days after the date the demand notice was mailed'. DOR Taxpayer Bill of Rights (https://secure.in.gov/dor/resources/tax-library/taxpayer-bill-of-rights/): 'If a liability is not paid or protested within 60 days of the first notice, DOR will issue a "Demand Notice" for payment before issuing a tax warrant.'
uncertainty: The statute was read on FindLaw, a secondary host. The official iga.in.gov site needs JavaScript. DOR's own pages confirm the 20 days and the 10%.
designImplication: For IN, the fuse is 60 days to the demand, then 20 days to the warrant. The warrant adds 10% of the unpaid tax at once.

claim: The IN notice before a lien is the Demand Notice (Demand for Payment). By statute it must state the 20 days to pay or show reasonable cause. It must also state DOR's authority to issue a warrant and to levy, the earliest date a warrant may be filed and recorded, and the remedies available to prevent the filing.

value.from: date the department mails the notice
mustState: 20 days to pay or show reasonable cause
statutory authority to issue a tax warrant
